newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: FOCUS - Dutch to slash debt to GDP ratio.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Dutch to slash debt to GDP ratio.

text.p: Dutch public sector debt is projected to fall to 76.2 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) next year from 78.8 percent this year, according to the 1997 budget unveiled by the government on Tuesday.

The reduction comes as no surprise as Finance Minister Gerrit Zalm had been expected to pursue a leaner debt ratio -- the only criterion for European economic and monetary union (EMU) posing serious problems for the Dutch.
The latest government figures show the debt ratio beginning to edge lower from 1996 after remaining stubbornly high at around 80 percent of GDP for most of the last decade.
Despite the sudden progress in reducing public sector debt ahead of the monetary union, Zalm denied the government had resorted to sleight-of-hand.

He told a pre-budget press briefing that roughly 60 percent of the decline in the debt ratio was attributable to budget discipline and economic growth while the remaining 40 percent reflected a one-off financial windfall.
Further structural reductions in public debt would be reflected even more strongly in the 1998 budget, Zalm added.
Budget documents show that a projected 5.0 percent rise in nominal GDP to 693.2 billion guilders in 1997 will help bring down the ratio of debt to GDP by boosting the denominator.
A reduction in the public sector deficit, another key EMU measure, to 2.2 percent of GDP from 2.6 percent in 1996 is also expected to check the rise of public debt relative to GDP.
Finally, the overall level of public debt will be reduced in 1997 by drawing down an obsolete government cash reserve held at the Dutch central bank, leading to a one-off windfall in 1997.
At 76.2 percent of GDP, the Dutch debt ratio will still be well above the EMU target of 60 percent.
But the Dutch are confident of qualifying for the third phase of EMU because they satisfy the other EMU targets for the deficit, inflation, interest rates and exchange rate stability.
